Remember one distinction: Critical Care Nurses keep unstable patients from crossing a dangerous threshold, while general nurses provide broader routine care. One manages the critical boundary; the other manages daily care.
This work does not suit people who fear blood, cannot tolerate shift work or death, or become emotionally overwhelmed. Long-term ICU work places heavy demands on both mental and physical health.
A common path is: study nursing → pass the nursing licensure examination → gain experience on a general ward → complete ICU specialty training → become a Critical Care Nurse.

This work suits people who remain emotionally steady, perform procedures accurately, and think clearly under pressure. If you insist on precision because every detail affects a life, you can build a stable career here.

Critical Care Nurses care for patients with unstable vital signs in intensive-care units. They provide continuous monitoring, precise medication, life-support equipment management, and complication prevention while collaborating with physicians during high-risk periods.

paragraphs: Begin each shift with handover and identify every patient's likely turning points. During rounds, review monitors, inspect lines, and adjust infusion rates. If oxygen saturation drops, assess immediately, suction the airway, and call the physician. Watch trend charts overnight and treat every small change seriously. At handover, communicate each risk point clearly.
